script.opening: "Hello doctor, thank you for ringing back. It’s… delicate. I’m calling about Tyler Brooks — he’s in my class, and I’m also meant to be the safeguarding lead, which is rather the problem. I know the family, you see. Socially. I’ve been going back and forth for two weeks about whether I’m imagining things, and I suppose I was hoping you could… look into it from your end? Quietly?"

facts.text: Hungry most mornings ("inhales the breakfast club toast"); new daytime wetting after years dry; the flinch at a raised male voice; shin bruising in odd places; "he’s gone quiet — he used to be the chattiest boy in the room".
All of it this term — which began around when mum’s new partner moved in. Tyler has mentioned "Gav doesn’t like noise".

Only if her discomfort is explored: she and Tyler’s mum were at school together; their families know each other; she’s frightened of being identified as the referrer, of "blowing up a family over toast and a bruise", and of being wrong in a small town.
Nothing formal yet. No referral to children’s social care. She’s logged notes "in my own notebook" — not the school system. The head "prefers things handled informally".
For the GP to "look into it" — examine Tyler at an asthma review, "see what you think" — so that any referral comes from the surgery, not from her.
She knows, really. "If a parent described this to me about another school’s child, I’d have referred a fortnight ago." Saying it out loud is what she needed.

ice.ideas: Something is wrong at home since "Gav" arrived — she’s pattern-matched it correctly and is fighting her own conclusion.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — she’s socially entangled with the family and terrified of being identified as the referrer in a small community. Her real request isn’t advice; it’s for the GP to take the referral off her hands so she never has to be "the one who reported them".
ice.expectations: That the GP will quietly investigate and refer if needed, letting the school stay out of it. Needs to leave the call understanding that her duty doesn’t transfer — but that she won’t carry it alone.

cues: "I know the family, you see. Socially." — the entanglement, declared in the second sentence and shaping everything after.
"In my own notebook" — concerns kept OFF the school’s system; the informal-handling culture is itself a finding.
"If a parent described this to me about another school’s child…" — she already knows; she needs permission to act on it.

checkpoints.text: Listens fully and takes the concerns seriously as a safeguarding pattern: new hunger + secondary enuresis + flinching + unexplained bruising + behavioural change + new male partner in the home — names it as meeting the threshold for referral
Holds confidentiality correctly both ways: receives all information freely, shares nothing about Tyler or the family beyond what safeguarding requires — and says which is which
Reviews and contributes the GP-side picture: the bunk-bed A&E attendance, the DNA’d reviews, the health-visitor note — recognising the records corroborate rather than reassure

Is clear on the law of it: her safeguarding duty as DSL is hers and does not transfer — the school refers to children’s social care; the GP makes their OWN referral in parallel and shares information lawfully; neither waits for the other
Explores the hesitation and finds the entanglement — the friendship, the small town, the head’s "informal" culture — without shaming her for two lost weeks

Gives her what she actually needs: her own sentence reflected back ("you said it yourself — another school’s child, you’d have referred a fortnight ago") plus the facts that protect her (referrals can be managed sensitively; being wrong kindly beats being right too late)

Addresses the notebook and the head’s culture directly but constructively: concerns belong on the school’s formal system today; anyone can refer to children’s social care directly, so the head’s permission is not needed, and the chair of governors is the route if the head obstructs (the LADO handles allegations against staff, not a head who won’t refer)

Closes with parallel, dated actions: she refers to children’s social care today and logs formally; the GP reviews the family records, makes the practice’s own referral, flags the siblings, and books Tyler’s "asthma review" as a legitimate clinical contact — with a same-day escalation line if Tyler presents injured or afraid to go home

worked.txt: "You can tell me all of it — information coming TO me breaches nothing. What I can’t do is hand you details back about the family. So pour it out, and then we’ll sort out who does what."

"Listed together — the hunger, the wetting after years dry, the flinch, the bruising, the silence, all starting when a new partner moved in — that’s not toast and a bruise. That’s a pattern that crosses the referral line, and I think you know it does."

"You said something important: another school’s child, you’d have referred two weeks ago. The friendship hasn’t changed what Tyler needs — it’s changed how much it costs YOU. Those are different problems, and I can help with the second one."

"Here’s the part I can’t soften: the referral duty you hold as safeguarding lead is yours, and it doesn’t transfer to me. What I CAN promise is that you won’t act alone — the practice will make its own referral today, in parallel. Two referrals are stronger than one, and neither of us waits for the other."

"The notebook worries me almost as much as the bruises — concerns that live in your handbag protect nobody and expose you completely. Today they go on the school’s formal system, dated. And if the head wants it ‘informal’, you don’t need permission to refer — anyone can — and your chair of governors is there if it comes to it."

"Two more things before you go. If Tyler ever comes in injured, or says he’s scared to go home — that’s not a referral, that’s a same-day call to children’s services and they will tell you about police involvement. And ring me after you’ve referred — I want to know it’s done, and I want you to hear that you did right by him."

f.learning: A third-party safeguarding call runs on three rails at once: information flows IN freely (and the GP’s own records — the implausible A&E story, the DNAs, the HV note — corroborate); confidentiality flows OUT only as safeguarding lawfully requires; and duties never transfer — the DSL refers, the practice refers in parallel, neither waits. The hidden agenda is the caller’s: social entanglement and an "informal" school culture have paralysed her for two weeks, and the consultation’s real work is converting her own sentence into her own referral, today, without shame.

points.t: NICE CG89 lists alerting features including unexplained bruising, secondary wetting, persistent hunger and fearful or withdrawn behaviour. Individually soft; together, new this term with a new adult in the home, they meet the referral threshold.
An A&E attendance with an injury explanation, missed health appointments and a health visitor note about household change add weight. Review the whole family’s records, including the sibling.

Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026: each professional acts on their own concern and anyone can refer to children’s social care. KCSIE 2026 places the referral responsibility on the school’s DSL.

Information can be received freely. The GP shares the child’s or family’s information only with children’s social care and other agencies as safeguarding requires, not with the caller (GMC Protecting children and young people, 2012).
Make the practice’s referral, document the call, code the records, flag siblings, and create legitimate clinical contact — not a covert examination without safeguarding advice (NICE NG76).
Disclosure, visible injury, or a child afraid to go home → same-day children’s social care contact; immediate danger → 999.

New partner in the home, younger sibling, the caller’s social ties, the school’s informal culture.

Physical abuse and neglect considered; alternative explanations acknowledged without letting them delay referral.
Asked about disclosures; same-day triggers named (injury, fear of going home, immediate danger).
Stated the cluster meets the threshold for referral to children’s social care.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

Overdue asthma care addressed; younger sibling considered.
Call-back once she has referred; same-day escalation named; documented the call.

Her idea (something is wrong since the partner arrived), concern (being identified as referrer), expectation (the GP takes it over).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan

Her real request isn’t advice; it’s for the GP to take the referral off her hands so she never has to be "the one who reported them" — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, it’s Dr Lee returning your call from the surgery. Can I confirm who I’m speaking to and your role at the school?
model.why: Confirms identity and role before any discussion

model.text: Angela Reeve. I’m Tyler Brooks’s class teacher, and the designated safeguarding lead — which is rather the problem. I know the family, you see. Socially. I was hoping you could look into it from your end. Quietly?

Thank you for calling. Let me be clear about how this works: you can tell me everything — information coming to me breaches nothing. I can’t share details about the family back with you. Then we’ll agree who does what. Is that all right?
model.why: Sets out confidentiality in both directions at the start

model.text: Yes. That’s fair.
Tell me what you’ve noticed about Tyler, from the beginning.
model.why: Open question; lets her give the full account

model.text: He arrives hungry most mornings — inhales the breakfast club toast. He’s started wetting himself again after years dry. He flinched badly when a male assistant raised his voice. There’s bruising on his shin I couldn’t make sense of. And he’s gone quiet — he was the chattiest boy in the room.
When did these changes start? Has Tyler said anything himself?
All this term. About when his mum’s new partner moved in. Tyler said once, “Gav doesn’t like noise.”
Where are these concerns recorded, and what’s been done so far?
model.why: Checks what action and documentation already exist

model.text: Nothing formal. They’re in my own notebook. The head prefers things handled informally.
You mentioned you know the family socially. How is that affecting all this for you?
model.why: Follows the cue in her second sentence

model.text: His mum and I were at school together. It’s a small town. If I’m wrong, I’ve blown up a family over toast and a bruise. And if I’m right, everyone knows it was me.
That’s a real bind, and it makes sense you’ve gone back and forth. Can I ask — if another school’s teacher described this child to you, what would you advise?
model.why: Helps her reach her own professional judgement without shaming

model.text: (Pause.) I’d have told them to refer a fortnight ago.

I agree with you. Hunger, wetting after years dry, flinching, unexplained bruising and a quiet boy — all starting when a new adult moved in. Taken together, that crosses the line for a referral to children’s social care. Your friendship hasn’t changed what Tyler needs; it’s changed what it costs you.
model.why: Names the pattern as meeting the referral threshold

model.text: So you’ll refer?

I will make the practice’s own referral today, because I have information you don’t. But your duty as safeguarding lead is yours and doesn’t transfer to me. We both refer, today, and neither waits for the other. Two referrals are stronger than one.
model.why: Clarifies that duties do not transfer; parallel referrals

model.text: I was hoping you’d say it could come from you.

I understand. Social care are used to handling referrals sensitively, and a professional referral doesn’t mean your name is shared with the family. Being wrong kindly is far better than being right too late — for Tyler and for you.
model.why: Addresses her fear with accurate reassurance

model.text: Two more things. The notebook: today those notes go onto the school’s safeguarding record, dated. And the head’s preference doesn’t override your duty — anyone can refer to children’s social care directly, and if leadership obstructs, your chair of governors is the route.
model.why: Addresses the informal culture constructively and accurately

model.text: The chair of governors. Right. I can do that.

On my side, I’ll review the family’s records, flag his younger sibling, and offer Tyler an asthma review as a normal appointment, following safeguarding advice. If Tyler comes in injured, or says he’s scared to go home, that’s a same-day call to children’s social care — or 999 if he’s in immediate danger.
model.why: GP actions, sibling flagged, and same-day escalation triggers

model.text: Understood.
Can you tell me back what you’ll do after this call?
Refer to children’s social care today. Put everything on the school system. Governors if the head pushes back. Same-day call if he’s hurt or scared.
Exactly. Ring me once you’ve referred, so we both know it’s done. You’ve done right by him by calling.
model.why: Closes the loop and supports the caller

social.t: A new adult in the home, a younger sibling and missed health appointments are recognised contexts for maltreatment; all children in the household are considered.
Professional and social roles overlap. Fear of being identified is common; referrals from professionals are handled sensitively.

legal.t: Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026 (DfE): anyone with concerns can refer to local authority children’s social care, and each agency acts on its own concerns. Keeping Children Safe in Education 2026 (in force 1 September 2026) sets the DSL’s responsibilities.

The GP may share information with children’s social care to safeguard a child, including without parental consent where seeking it would increase risk (GMC Protecting children and young people, 2012; Data Protection Act 2018).
Section 47 enquiries are led by children’s social care where there is reasonable cause to suspect significant harm; the GP contributes information.

professional.t: Record the call contemporaneously: caller, role, what was reported, advice given and actions agreed. Code the child’s record and link the sibling’s.
The LADO handles allegations against adults who work with children. A head preferring informality is a governance issue for the governing body, not a LADO matter.

community.t: Practice safeguarding lead and named GP for advice; local safeguarding children partnership procedures; NSPCC helpline for professionals seeking advice.

redFlags: Disclosure by the child, visible injury, or a child afraid to go home — same-day children’s social care contact
Implausible injury explanation on record, missed appointments, younger sibling in the household
psychosocial: New partner in the home this term
Caller’s social ties to the family and fear of being identified
ice: Idea: something is wrong at home since “Gav” moved in
Concern: being identified as the referrer in a small town, or being wrong
Expectation: the GP quietly investigates and refers instead of her

playbook.diagnosis: A cluster of new concerns (hunger, secondary wetting, flinching, unexplained bruising, withdrawal) coinciding with a new adult in the home, corroborated by GP records — meets the threshold for referral to children’s social care for suspected abuse or neglect.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Any one of these on its own might have an innocent explanation. All of them together, starting at the same time, is the kind of pattern that has to be looked at properly by children’s services.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried about being the one who reported them. You won’t be acting alone — I’m referring too, today.”
management.psychosocial: Support the caller: acknowledge the bind, remove shame about the delay, reflect her own judgement, and agree a call-back.
sharedPlan: School DSL refers to children’s social care today and moves notes onto the school record
GP makes the practice’s own referral today, reviews the family’s records and flags the sibling
Asthma review offered to Tyler as a normal appointment, following safeguarding advice
safetyNet: Injury, disclosure or fear of going home — same-day children’s social care; immediate danger — 999
Call-back once her referral is made; governors if leadership obstructs

pitfalls.intro: This station tests professional judgement more than clinical knowledge. It is failed by accepting the duty transfer, breaching confidentiality, or leaving without a referral in motion.

items.fail: Agreeing to “look into it quietly” at the next asthma review.
items.why: Delays action and accepts a duty transfer the law does not allow (Working Together 2026).
items.fix: “This meets the threshold. You refer today, and I’ll make the practice’s referral too.”

items.fail: Sharing record details with the caller — the A&E attendance, the new partner.
items.why: Breaches confidentiality; she is not the route for the family’s information.
items.fix: Receive everything; include relevant record details in your own referral to social care.

items.why: Concerns about one child in the household extend to all children in it.
items.fix: Flag the sibling’s record and mention them in the referral.

items.fail: Criticising her for the two-week delay.
items.why: “Does not show sensitivity.” Shame paralyses rather than mobilises.
items.fix: Reflect her own words: “You said you’d have advised another school to refer.”

items.fail: Ignoring the notebook and the head’s informal culture.
items.why: Leaves the concerns off the formal record and the barrier in place.
items.fix: Notes on the school system today; anyone can refer; governors if leadership obstructs.

items.fail: Ending with “let’s both have a think”.
items.why: No dated actions; each professional assumes the other will act.
items.fix: Dated parallel actions, same-day triggers and a call-back to confirm the referral is made.

wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explores her entanglement without shame; reflects her own professional judgement back; corrects the duty transfer clearly and kindly; addresses the notebook and the informal culture; flags the sibling; closes with dated parallel actions and a call-back.

avoid.instead: “This meets the threshold now. You refer today, and so will I.”
avoid.why: Delay and duty transfer are the classic failure of multi-agency safeguarding.

avoid.dont: “Actually, the notes show he was in A&E recently with his arm.”
avoid.instead: “I’ll review our records and include what’s relevant in my own referral.”
avoid.why: Sharing the family’s records with the caller is a confidentiality breach.

avoid.why: Shaming the caller makes her less likely to act.

legal.t: Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026 (DfE): anyone with concerns can refer to local authority children’s social care, and each agency acts on its own concerns. Keeping Children Safe in Education 2026 (in force 1 September 2026) sets the DSL’s responsibilities.

The GP may share information with children’s social care to safeguard a child, including without parental consent where seeking it would increase risk (GMC Protecting children and young people, 2012; Data Protection Act 2018).
Section 47 enquiries are led by children’s social care where there is reasonable cause to suspect significant harm; the GP contributes information.

professional.t: Record the call contemporaneously: caller, role, what was reported, advice given and actions agreed. Code the child’s record and link the sibling’s.
The LADO handles allegations against adults who work with children. A head preferring informality is a governance issue for the governing body, not a LADO matter.

community.t: Practice safeguarding lead and named GP for advice; local safeguarding children partnership procedures; NSPCC helpline for professionals seeking advice.

redFlags: Disclosure by the child, visible injury, or a child afraid to go home — same-day children’s social care contact
Implausible injury explanation on record, missed appointments, younger sibling in the household
psychosocial: New partner in the home this term
Caller’s social ties to the family and fear of being identified
ice: Idea: something is wrong at home since “Gav” moved in
Concern: being identified as the referrer in a small town, or being wrong
Expectation: the GP quietly investigates and refers instead of her

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: A cluster of new concerns (hunger, secondary wetting, flinching, unexplained bruising, withdrawal) coinciding with a new adult in the home, corroborated by GP records — meets the threshold for referral to children’s social care for suspected abuse or neglect.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Any one of these on its own might have an innocent explanation. All of them together, starting at the same time, is the kind of pattern that has to be looked at properly by children’s services.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried about being the one who reported them. You won’t be acting alone — I’m referring too, today.”
management.psychosocial: Support the caller: acknowledge the bind, remove shame about the delay, reflect her own judgement, and agree a call-back.
sharedPlan: School DSL refers to children’s social care today and moves notes onto the school record
GP makes the practice’s own referral today, reviews the family’s records and flags the sibling
Asthma review offered to Tyler as a normal appointment, following safeguarding advice
safetyNet: Injury, disclosure or fear of going home — same-day children’s social care; immediate danger — 999
Call-back once her referral is made; governors if leadership obstructs

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests professional judgement more than clinical knowledge. It is failed by accepting the duty transfer, breaching confidentiality, or leaving without a referral in motion.

items.fail: Agreeing to “look into it quietly” at the next asthma review.
items.why: Delays action and accepts a duty transfer the law does not allow (Working Together 2026).
items.fix: “This meets the threshold. You refer today, and I’ll make the practice’s referral too.”

items.fail: Sharing record details with the caller — the A&E attendance, the new partner.
items.why: Breaches confidentiality; she is not the route for the family’s information.
items.fix: Receive everything; include relevant record details in your own referral to social care.

items.why: Concerns about one child in the household extend to all children in it.
items.fix: Flag the sibling’s record and mention them in the referral.

items.fail: Criticising her for the two-week delay.
items.why: “Does not show sensitivity.” Shame paralyses rather than mobilises.
items.fix: Reflect her own words: “You said you’d have advised another school to refer.”

items.fail: Ignoring the notebook and the head’s informal culture.
items.why: Leaves the concerns off the formal record and the barrier in place.
items.fix: Notes on the school system today; anyone can refer; governors if leadership obstructs.

items.fail: Ending with “let’s both have a think”.
items.why: No dated actions; each professional assumes the other will act.
items.fix: Dated parallel actions, same-day triggers and a call-back to confirm the referral is made.
